executive_assessment.text: Named northern and central water-stressed areas face differentiated livelihood, nutrition and service-access constraints, with most local indicators dating to 2015/16–2022.

Pastoral mobility is an established coping strategy. A localized IFRC assessment associates drought-related movement with resource competition and unspecified conflict; human–wildlife conflict is a separate finding.

Finance and insurance access, local response authority, early-action delays and distribution safeguards constrain capacity. Reported historical interventions and 2024/25 response reach do not establish sustained recovery.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2021-07 reports: The diagnostic identifies the central area, Walvis Bay–Swakopmund coast and Cuvelai as highly water-stressed; northern regions have the largest shares lacking safe water and sanitation.

Source dated 2021-07 reports: The report’s 2015/16 profile places poverty above the national average in Kavango East, Kunene, Omaheke and Zambezi; poor groups included children, older people and female-headed households.

Source dated 2023-01 reports: In 2021/22, delayed rains and prolonged dry spells left crop areas with below-average harvests, including northern Kunene and Omusati and parts of Oshana and Otjozondjupa.

Source dated 2023-01 reports: NAMVAC reported ongoing drought effects in Kunene, Erongo and Omusati; Kunene had eight consecutive drought years, with livestock deaths, lost income and depleted grazing and water.
Source dated 2023-01 reports: In 2022, households consuming only zero to two food groups were most prevalent in Kunene (42%), Kavango East (39.7%), Oshikoto (30.4%) and Kavango West (29.7%).
Source dated 2022 reports: IFRC names Kunene, Erongo, Omusati and Omaheke as drought-prone; communal crop/livestock households were heavily affected.
Source dated 2022 reports: Women spent longer fetching water; children sometimes left school as pastoral households moved, and many such households were female-headed.
Source dated 2022 reports: Red Cross actions included Kunene borehole repairs, solar pumps, WASH outreach and cash aid in 2019–21.

Source dated 2023 reports: The 2023 diagnostic found agricultural insurance largely limited to commercial farmers; proposed or tested drought-index products included options for communal farmers in Kavango East, Kavango West and Zambezi.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification. Routine/default app-use approval does not certify claims or sources. 18 of 19 evidence records and 1 of 1 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
Local evidence is strongest for Kunene and Omusati in a small IFRC assessment; the 2026 after-action review and other national sources provide limited site-level outcome data.
The UN Namibia Common Country Analysis 2023 PDF exceeded the web reader's size limit, and the official-host BTR1/NC5 PDF URL returned 404; neither was used as evidence.
NAMVAC 2022/23 and IFRC 2022 findings are dated; the 2026 after-action review is retrospective and does not provide named regional outcome estimates.

The IFRC assessment describes both human–wildlife conflict and pastoral mobility associated with resource competition. The latter does not specify conflict type or scale; neither supports an armed-conflict or migrant-threat inference.
No verified conflict-to-adaptation pathway was found. Local evidence is selective, while the 2026 after-action review is retrospective and mostly national.
Historical poverty, food-security and service indicators are not current 2026 prevalence. IPC projection for January–March 2023 was excluded.
Reported aid reach and water-response benefits are assessment findings, not measured lasting recovery or counterfactual impacts.
